title: Moses is rebuked
hookLine: a voice tells Moses he was sent to join people to God, not to part them (Masnavi 2)

cards: Maybe you've been corrected at a moment you were trying your hardest. You cooked for someone and they told you how their mother makes it. You finally opened up about something and got a lecture back.
The correction might even have been right. But something closed, and it didn't open again for a long time. Moses, presumably, walked on feeling he'd done his job.
Then he hears a voice, and it isn't pleased with him.

teach.h: YOU HAVE PARTED MY SERVANT FROM ME.
teach.b: In Rumi's telling, a revelation comes to Moses from God, something like this. You have parted my servant from me. Did you come as a prophet to bring people together, or to split them apart?

teach.h: YOU CAME TO UNITE, NOT TO SEVER.
teach.b: Rumi puts it in a rhyming couplet: you came to unite, not to sever. Then the voice goes on. I have given every person a way of their own, a way of speaking.
What is praise from him would be blame from you. What's honey for one is poison for another.

teach.h: I LOOK AT THE HEART, NOT THE TONGUE.
teach.b: And then the turn: I don't look at the tongue and the words. I look at the heart and its state.

Rumi gives an example from his own world: the idiom of India is praise for the people of India, the idiom of Sind for the people of Sind. Different words, the same longing. Notice what the story doesn't say.
It doesn't say Moses was wrong that God has no body; Rumi's tradition keeps that teaching. It says Moses was wrong to make the shepherd's words the test of his heart. The man's language was mistaken.
His love was not. That's hard for anyone who loves getting things right. The story isn't against correct teaching.
It's a warning about what correction can cost when it lands on someone who is only trying to love.
So when you hear someone pray or talk about the sacred in a way that isn't yours, the story suggests a first thought: their words, not mine.

how: Readers of Rumi often cite this story when they talk about respecting other people's ways of prayer, and many Sufi teachers use it to warn against judging sincerity by vocabulary.

o: a short Persian song of praise

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.
p: praise for the people of Sind

s: the story says Moses was wrong that God has no body
Rumi keeps that teaching. Moses was wrong to judge the shepherd's heart by his words.
the voice says what's praise from one may be blame from another
every person is given their own way of speaking.
the rebuke comes from the shepherd
it comes to Moses as a revelation from God.

games.q: you're Moses. you've just corrected a shepherd's prayer, and a voice from God asks you why. what does the voice say you were sent to do?
o: to bring people together with God, not split them apart.
games.why: you came to unite, not to sever. in Rumi's Persian, the two halves rhyme.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose way with the sacred is different from yours: a grandmother with her beads, a friend who talks to the universe, a colleague who fasts, a child at bedtime.
Picture them in the middle of it, and don't correct anything, even inside. Just listen for the heart underneath the words.

wordCard.voice: Vasl, Persian for union: the voice tells Moses he was sent to join people to God, not to part them, and that God looks at the heart, not the tongue. Today's word.

orig.note: Persian, from Arabic: union, joining. 'you came to join (vasl), not to sever (fasl).'

carryVoice: Your line: their words, not mine. God looks at the heart. Day one hundred ninety-five, done.

sources.ref: Masnavi Book 2, after 2.1720 (God's rebuke of Moses)
